topic: std::async Default Policy: Delegating Thread Management
explanation: Assumption: Calling `std::async(f)` guarantees that the function `f` will immediately run on a separate, concurrent thread. Reality: The default launch policy is `std::launch::async | std::launch::deferred`. This means the task may run asynchronously immediately, or its execution may be postponed (deferred) until the program calls `wait()` or `get()` on the returned `std::future`. Why It Works: This flexibility allows the C++ Standard Library to assume responsibility for crucial thread management tasks, including load balancing, preventing oversubscription, and optimizing thread creation/destruction overhead.
code_example:
auto fut1 = std::async(f); // Uses default policy
// fut1 might run immediately, or it might wait until fut1.get() is called.
practical_example: A developer expects a function to start heavy computation immediately upon calling `std::async`. If the system is highly loaded, the Standard Library might choose deferred execution, causing the computation to block the main thread later when results are requested via `get()`.
chapter: Item 36: Understand std::async behavior under default launch policy
